results.reason: The memo cites §2.2's automatic renewal for successive five-year periods and the 270/240-day window. It calculates the window as October 3 to November 2, 2026 against the June 30, 2027 expiry. It explains the lock-in through June 30, 2032 with the minimum commitments, and recommends serving protective notice or obtaining a written amendment before November 2.

The memo identifies the §5.3 30-day objection and removal right with deemed acceptance. It notes the 14% increase effective November 1, 2026, receipt on August 21, 2026, and the September 20, 2026 deadline. It concludes the right has almost certainly lapsed, recommends confirming with the client whether an objection was sent, and suggests negotiating a concession.

The memo explains that §11.1 is broad enough to cover Brightmere-caused claims such as design defects and failure to warn, that §12.3(a) makes it uncapped, and that Brightmere's §11.2 indemnity is narrow and capped. It recommends narrowing §11.1 to Halvorsen's own fault and making the indemnity mutual or capped.

The memo identifies that First Amendment §3 deletes and replaces §12.3 and drops the recall carve-out. It explains that recall reimbursement is now subject to the 12-month fees cap, which a large recall could exceed, and recommends reinstating the carve-out.

The memo identifies First Amendment §6 as selecting Delaware law and exclusive Wilmington jurisdiction, in conflict with §§17.1–17.2 (New York). It states the amendment prevails under §1.4 and recommends conforming governing law and forum back to New York.
The memo states that the notice was received on August 21, 2026.
The memo states that the Initial Term ends June 30, 2027.
The memo states that under §1.4 written amendments take precedence over the Agreement body.
The response is a memo addressed to the Supervising Partner. Each issue has a Where (document and section), a Why it matters, and a Recommended fix.
The memo expressly states that recall reimbursement can no longer be treated as outside the cap.
The memo concludes that Delaware law and forum now govern under the amendment, and does not conclude that New York law and forum still apply.
